meta.title: Python Fundamentals - Interview Questions
meta.description: 30 mostly asked Python Fundamentals interview questions with easy, detailed explanations and practical code examples.

questions.question: What is the difference between mutable and immutable objects in Python?

answer.short_answer: A **mutable** object can be edited in place after it is created. An **immutable** object can never change, so an operation that looks like an edit actually builds a **new** object and moves the name onto it.
answer.detailed_explanation:
A name in Python is only a label. It points at an object in memory, and operations never change the label itself. They either **edit the object the label points to**, or **move the label to a different object**. That single distinction is the whole idea behind mutability.

- **Mutable** objects have methods that change their own contents, such as `append`, `remove`, `update`, `add` and `clear`.
- **Immutable** objects have no such methods. `s.upper()` reads like an edit, but it returns a new object and discards the original.

So the quick test is this: after the operation, **is the original object different?** If it is, the object was mutable.

A useful side effect of immutability is safe sharing. If a hundred functions hold the same string, none of them can damage it for the others. That is exactly why `str`, `int`, `tuple` and `frozenset` are immutable, and why a `tuple` can be a dictionary key while a `list` cannot.

code_examples.title: Mutable: the object itself is edited
code_examples.code:
items = [1, 2, 3]
items.append(4)
print(items)
code_examples.explanation: append() edits the existing list, so the same object now holds four items.

code_examples.title: Immutable: a brand new object is built
code_examples.code:
text = 'Python'
text = text + ' 3'
print(text)
code_examples.explanation: The old string is untouched. Python built a second string and moved the name text onto it.

code_examples.title: Proof with id(): the same object was edited
code_examples.code:
items = [1, 2]
before = id(items)
items.append(3)
print(before == id(items))
code_examples.explanation: The id never changed, which proves the list was edited in place rather than replaced.

important_points: `x = 5` does not store 5 inside the variable. It binds the name x to an int object that holds 5.
Assignment `b = a` never copies anything. It simply adds a second name for the same object.
Immutable does not mean the value is constant for the whole program. The name can still be re-bound to a new object at any time.
A tuple is an immutable container, but the objects inside it can be mutable. `(1, [2])` can never change its slots, yet the list inside it can.
Immutable objects are hashable by default, which is why they are allowed as dictionary keys and set members.
common_mistakes: Writing `lst2 = lst1` and expecting a copy. Use `lst1.copy()` for a shallow copy or `copy.deepcopy(lst1)` for a deep one.
Assuming a tuple makes the whole structure immutable. `t = (1, [2, 3])` still allows `t[1].append(4)`.
Calling `.sort()` on a string or a tuple. Only lists have sort().
Using a list as a dictionary key, which raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`.
answer.real_world_usage: Dictionaries and sets are mutable because data has to grow and shrink as it arrives, so caches, config maps and lookup tables all depend on mutability. Immutable values are preferred for anything shared: configuration read by several modules, dictionary keys, and any value handed to a function that must not be able to alter the caller's data. Tuples are used for fixed records and function return values precisely because they cannot change after creation.
answer.interview_tip: Do not stop at 'list is mutable, tuple is immutable'. The interviewer wants to hear that Python has no idea what a variable holds, only that a name is a reference to an object, and that `x = 5` re-binds the name rather than changing the number. Close with one line about why that makes immutable objects safe to share, and the answer is complete.

questions.question: What are mutable and immutable data types in Python?

answer.short_answer: **Mutable** types are `list`, `dict`, `set` and `bytearray`, plus your own class instances. **Immutable** types are `int`, `float`, `bool`, `complex`, `str`, `bytes`, `tuple`, `frozenset` and `None`.
answer.detailed_explanation:
Every built-in type sits on one side of this line, and you can check the side at runtime instead of memorising it. Just ask whether the object has methods that edit its own contents.

- **Mutable types** change in place: `list`, `dict`, `set`, `bytearray`. Your own classes are mutable by default as well.
- **Immutable types** never change: `int`, `float`, `bool`, `complex`, `str`, `bytes`, `tuple`, `frozenset`, and the `None` singleton.

Two details trip almost everyone up. First, `int` being immutable does not make your variable constant. Writing `x = 10` and then `x = 20` is perfectly legal, because immutability is a property of the object, not of the name. Second, immutability belongs to the container and not to what the container holds. A tuple can contain a list, and that list can still be changed.

code_examples.title: Two lines that look identical
code_examples.code:
items = [1, 2]
items[0] = 99            # fine, list is mutable
print(items)

pair = (1, 2)
pair[0] = 99             # TypeError
code_examples.output:
[99, 2]
TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment
code_examples.explanation: The first line edits the object in place. The second tries to do the same and Python refuses, because a tuple has no way to change itself.

code_examples.title: Hashability follows mutability
code_examples.code:
print({(1, 2): 'tuple key'})      # works
print({[1, 2]: 'list key'})       # TypeError
code_examples.explanation: A dict needs to know exactly where a key lives. If a key could mutate, that location would become wrong, so only immutable objects are accepted as keys.

code_examples.title: Your own class is mutable by default
code_examples.explanation: Plain classes are mutable. Locking a class down is a deliberate extra step, which is exactly why frozen dataclasses exist.

important_points: `int` is immutable, but `x = 1` followed by `x = 2` is not an error. You are binding the name to a different object.
Immutable types are hashable by default and mutable types are not. That is the rule behind dictionary keys and set members.
A tuple is an immutable container, yet the objects inside a tuple can still be mutable.
Your own classes are mutable unless you deliberately lock them down.
`None` is a singleton and immutable, so compare it with `is None` rather than `== None`.
common_mistakes: Assuming `x = 1` then `x = 2` breaks because ints are immutable. It does not.
Using a list or a dict as a dictionary key and hitting `TypeError: unhashable type`.
Believing a tuple freezes everything nested inside it.
Testing with `==` and concluding nothing changed, when the object identity actually did change.
answer.real_world_usage: Most application code works with mutable types because real data grows. Immutable types appear wherever a value must not drift: dictionary keys, set members, configuration read by many modules, and any value passed into a function that should not be able to alter the caller's data. Type hints lean on this too, because a frozen dataclass is far safer to pass around than a plain class.
answer.interview_tip: Say the list off your fingers in one breath: mutable are list, dict, set and bytearray; immutable are int, float, bool, complex, str, bytes, tuple and frozenset. Then add the line that lifts the answer above memorising, which is that immutable objects are hashable, and that is why they are allowed as dictionary keys.

questions.question: What is the difference between a list and a tuple?

answer.short_answer: Both are **ordered** collections that allow duplicates and support indexing. The real difference is mutability: a **list** can be edited in place, a **tuple** cannot. Use a list for a collection that changes, a tuple for a fixed shape.
answer.detailed_explanation:
They behave so much alike that this is asked more than any other comparison. Both preserve order, both allow duplicates, both support indexing, slicing and iteration, and both can hold mixed types.

The difference is that a list can change after it is created and a tuple cannot. That one fact cascades into almost everything else you need to know:

- A list cannot be a dictionary key or a set member, because it is unhashable. A tuple can be, provided all of its items are hashable.
- A tuple takes slightly less memory, because it does not have to carry spare capacity for future growth.
- Appending to a list is fast, because Python keeps spare room internally so the append usually avoids resizing.

So the practical rule is short. If the collection will change, use a list. If the shape is fixed and you want the reader to know it cannot change, use a tuple.

code_examples.title: Growing a list versus changing a tuple
code_examples.code:
numbers = [1, 2, 3]
numbers.append(4)     # fine
print(numbers)

pair = (1, 2, 3)
pair[0] = 99          # TypeError
code_examples.output:
[1, 2, 3, 4]
TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment
code_examples.explanation: The list grows in place. The tuple has no method that can change it, so Python refuses at the first sign of an in-place edit.

code_examples.title: The comma that catches everyone
code_examples.code:
not_a_tuple = (5)      # just the int 5
real_tuple = (5,)      # a one item tuple

print(type(not_a_tuple))
print(type(real_tuple))
code_examples.explanation: Parentheses alone do not make a tuple. Without the trailing comma, Python simply evaluates the single value and hands that back.

code_examples.title: A tuple works as a dictionary key
code_examples.explanation: A tuple of hashable items can be a key. A list cannot, because a mutable key could change while it is stored inside the dict.

important_points: A tuple literal needs a trailing comma to hold exactly one item: `(5,)` and not `(5)`.
A tuple is hashable only if every item inside it is hashable. A tuple holding a list is not hashable.
`sorted()` always returns a list. To get a sorted tuple use `tuple(sorted(values))`.
Returning several values from a function hands back a tuple, which is why you can unpack it directly.
Two tuples can be compared, and the comparison is element by element, left to right.
common_mistakes: Writing `(5)` and expecting a one item tuple.
Trying to call `append`, `remove` or `sort` on a tuple.
Assuming a tuple freezes the objects inside it. `t = ([1], [2])` still allows `t[0].append(9)`.
Forgetting that unpacking works on a list too, so `a, b = [1, 2]` is perfectly valid.
answer.real_world_usage: Tuples are the default shape for anything fixed: the multiple return values of a function, coordinates, database rows, and the keys of a dict when a compound key is needed. Lists are used for anything that grows, such as search results, cart items or a queue. Using a tuple for fixed data also gives a small performance win, because Python does not have to reserve spare capacity for growth.
answer.interview_tip: Start with the one real difference, mutability, and let the rest follow as consequences instead of listing them as unrelated facts. A strong finish is that a tuple can be a dict key while a list cannot, because only immutable objects are hashable. Say that and the interviewer knows you understand why, not just what.

questions.question: What is the difference between a list and a set?

answer.short_answer: A **list** is ordered, allows duplicates and is reached by index. A **set** is unordered, keeps only unique values and is built for fast membership tests. Use a list when position matters, a set when you need uniqueness or fast lookup.
answer.detailed_explanation:
Both hold a group of values, but they are built to answer different questions.

A list answers "what is at position 3?". It remembers the order you added things in, and it happily stores the same value many times. Reaching position 3 means walking from the front, so the work grows with the size of the list.

A set answers "is this value present?". It keeps each value only once, and it remembers where each one lives using that value's hash. Looking a value up is therefore close to constant time instead of a full scan.

Two consequences follow from that. Membership in a list is a linear scan, so `value in big_list` walks the entire list. Membership in a set is a direct jump into a hash slot. And `set(...)` is the classic way to strip duplicates and make repeated lookups cheap.

code_examples.title: Duplicates and order
code_examples.code:
values = [1, 2, 2, 3, 1]
print(values)            # duplicates and order kept

unique = set(values)
print(unique)            # duplicates removed
print(sorted(unique))    # sorted() brings the order back
code_examples.explanation: A set does not remember order, so wrapping it in sorted() is the standard way to get predictable output.

code_examples.title: The speed difference you can measure
code_examples.code:
items = list(range(100_000))
print(99_999 in items)     # walks the whole list

lookup = set(items)
print(99_999 in lookup)    # jumps straight to it
code_examples.explanation: Both answer True, but the list has to check element after element, while the set goes directly to the right slot.

code_examples.title: Set operations a list cannot do
code_examples.explanation: Union, intersection and difference come built into sets. With lists you would have to write those loops yourself.

important_points: Sets need hashable items, so a set of lists is not allowed, while a set of tuples is fine.
A set has no index. `values[0]` is a TypeError.
You cannot change the contents of a set in place. `add` and `remove` work, but there is no `set[0] = x`.
An empty set is `set()`, never `{}`. Curly braces create an empty dict.
To get order back, wrap it: `sorted(myset)`.
common_mistakes: Writing `s = {}` and expecting a set. That is an empty dict, so use `set()`.
Trying `myset[0]`, or expecting `add` to preserve the order you added things in.
Putting an unhashable item such as a list inside a set and getting `TypeError: unhashable type`.
Using a list for heavy membership checks and then wondering why the loop feels slow.
answer.real_world_usage: Sets are the natural choice for de-duplicating records, tracking which ids have already been seen, cleaning duplicates out of user input, and comparing two collections such as the follower lists of two accounts. Lists remain right whenever order carries meaning, like a ranked results page or a transaction history.
answer.interview_tip: The strongest version of this answer explains the speed. Say that a set stores values in hash slots, so membership is roughly O(1), while a list has to be scanned, which is O(n). That one sentence shows you understand the data structure, and it is the part the interviewer is listening for.

questions.question: What is the difference between a list and a dictionary?

answer.short_answer: A **list** is a sequence reached by position, so `items[0]` is the first item. A **dict** is a mapping reached by key, so `user['name']` is the value stored under that key. Use a list when order and position matter, a dict when each value has a meaningful label.
answer.detailed_explanation:
The difference is not really about speed, it is about what you use to reach the value.

A list is indexed by position, and positions are counted from zero. That is fine when the items are interchangeable, like a list of scores, but it is awkward when every item has a name. If the order changes, each index that pointed at the right thing now points at the wrong thing.

A dict is indexed by key. Instead of remembering that the name sits at index 1, you ask for the name directly. The order of the keys becomes an implementation detail rather than something your code depends on.

A good rule is to ask how you would describe the item. If the honest answer is "the third one", use a list. If the answer is something meaningful like a user id or a country code, use a dict.

code_examples.title: Position versus name
code_examples.code:
students = ['Amit', 'Abhi', 'Rahul']
print(students[1])        # by position

student = {'name': 'Abhi', 'age': 21}
print(student['name'])    # by key
code_examples.explanation: The same answer, but the list only works if you remember the position, while the dict asks for the thing you actually want.

code_examples.title: What happens when the key is missing
code_examples.code:
prices = {'pen': 10}
print(prices['pen'])

# print(prices['book'])   # KeyError
print(prices.get('book', 0))   # 0
code_examples.explanation: Indexing with a missing key raises KeyError. The get method is the safe way to read a value that may not be there.

code_examples.title: Building a dict from pairs
code_examples.code:
pairs = [('name', 'Abhi'), ('age', 21)]
print(dict(pairs))

squares = {n: n * n for n in range(5)}
print(squares)
code_examples.explanation: A dict can be built from key value pairs, and the dict comprehension is the readable way to build one inside a loop.

important_points: Dict keys must be hashable and unique. Writing the same key twice simply overwrites the old value.
Iterating a dict gives you the keys. Use `data.values()` or `data.items()` when you need the rest.
Since Python 3.7 a dict keeps insertion order, so output is predictable, but the key is still how you look things up.
`data.keys()` returns a view rather than a copy, so it reflects changes made to the dict afterwards.
A list index is a position while a dict key is a label. Confusing the two is the most common bug in this area.
common_mistakes: Using `data[0]` and expecting the first item. A dict is not indexable by position.
Writing `data.keys()[0]`, which fails because keys() returns a view, not a list.
Letting a missing key raise KeyError in production code instead of reaching for get.
Keeping parallel lists such as a names list and an ages list, instead of a list of dicts or a dict of lists.
answer.real_world_usage: A dict is the default choice whenever data carries labels, which is most real application code: JSON payloads, database rows turned into records, configuration, and counting with `collections.Counter`. Lists stay the right tool for sequences where order is the point, such as a feed of results, a queue or a history.
answer.interview_tip: Do not answer this as a speed comparison, because that is the weaker answer. Say that a list is indexed by position and a dict is indexed by key, then give one sentence about why keys are better once the order can change. Finish with the practical rule: if you would describe the item by a name, use a dict; if you would describe it by its position, use a list.

questions.question: What is the difference between append(), extend(), and insert()?

answer.short_answer: append() adds one object at the end, extend() adds elements from an iterable, and insert() adds one object at a specified index.
answer.detailed_explanation: append(x) treats x as one element even when x is another list. extend(iterable) iterates over the supplied iterable and adds its elements one by one. insert(index, value) places one value before the specified position. All three modify the existing list and return None.

code_examples.title: append()
code_examples.code:
a = [1, 2]
a.append([3, 4])
print(a)
code_examples.explanation: The whole [3, 4] list becomes one element.

code_examples.title: extend()
code_examples.code:
a = [1, 2]
a.extend([3, 4])
print(a)
code_examples.explanation: The elements 3 and 4 are added individually.

code_examples.title: insert()
code_examples.code:
a = [1, 3]
a.insert(1, 2)
print(a)
code_examples.explanation: The value 2 is inserted at index 1.

questions.question: What is the difference between remove(), pop(), and del?

answer.short_answer: remove() deletes the first matching value, pop() removes and returns an item by index, and del is a statement that can delete an item, slice, or name.
answer.detailed_explanation: remove(value) is value-based and raises ValueError if the value is not found. pop(index) is index-based and returns the removed element; without an index it removes the last element. del can delete indexed elements, slices, or even a variable binding, but it does not return the deleted value. Knowing whether an operation is value-based, index-based, or a deletion statement is the key interview distinction.

code_examples.title: remove()
code_examples.code:
items = ['a', 'b', 'c']
items.remove('b')
print(items)
code_examples.explanation: It removes the first matching value.

code_examples.title: pop()
code_examples.code:
items = ['a', 'b', 'c']
removed = items.pop(1)
print(removed)
print(items)
code_examples.explanation: It removes index 1 and returns the removed value.

code_examples.title: del
code_examples.code:
items = ['a', 'b', 'c']
del items[1]
print(items)
code_examples.explanation: del removes the item without returning it.

questions.question: What is the difference between sort() and sorted()?

answer.short_answer: sort() sorts a list in place and returns None, while sorted() returns a new sorted list and works with any iterable.
answer.detailed_explanation: list.sort() changes the original list. sorted() leaves the original object unchanged and returns a new list. Both support key= and reverse=. Use sort() when modifying the existing list is intended. Use sorted() when you need to preserve the original data or when the input is another iterable such as a tuple or set.

code_examples.title: sort()
code_examples.code:
numbers = [3, 1, 2]
result = numbers.sort()
print(numbers)
print(result)
code_examples.explanation: sort() changes the list and returns None.

code_examples.title: sorted()
code_examples.code:
numbers = [3, 1, 2]
result = sorted(numbers)
print(numbers)
print(result)
code_examples.explanation: sorted() creates and returns a new list.

questions.question: What is the difference between reverse() and reversed()?

answer.short_answer: reverse() reverses a list in place and returns None, while reversed() returns an iterator that produces items in reverse order without modifying the original sequence.
answer.detailed_explanation: list.reverse() is a list method and directly changes the list. reversed() is a built-in function that works with reversible objects and returns an iterator. Convert the iterator to list() when you need a new list. The distinction is similar to sort() versus sorted(): one mutates a list, while the other produces a separate iterable result.

code_examples.title: reverse()
code_examples.code:
items = [1, 2, 3]
result = items.reverse()
print(items)
print(result)
code_examples.explanation: The original list is modified.

code_examples.title: reversed()
code_examples.code:
items = [1, 2, 3]
result = list(reversed(items))
print(items)
print(result)
code_examples.explanation: The original remains unchanged and reversed() supplies an iterator.

questions.question: What is list slicing in Python?

answer.short_answer: List slicing extracts part of a list using list[start:stop:step]. The start is included, stop is excluded, and step controls the jump between elements.
answer.detailed_explanation: Slicing creates a new list containing the selected elements. If start is omitted, slicing begins at the start; if stop is omitted, it continues to the end; step defaults to 1. Negative indexes can count from the end and a negative step can move backward. A common interview point is that normal list slicing creates a shallow copy of the selected portion, not a deep copy of nested objects.

code_examples.title: Basic Slice
code_examples.code:
numbers = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
print(numbers[1:4])
code_examples.explanation: Index 1 is included and index 4 is excluded.

code_examples.title: Step and Reverse
code_examples.code:
numbers = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
print(numbers[::2])
print(numbers[::-1])
code_examples.explanation: A step of 2 selects every second item; -1 traverses the list backward.

questions.question: What is negative indexing in Python?

answer.short_answer: Negative indexing accesses sequence elements from the end. -1 means the last item, -2 means the second-last item, and so on.
answer.detailed_explanation: Negative indexing works with common sequences such as lists, tuples, and strings. It is useful when you want the last few elements without calculating len(sequence). An index outside the valid range raises IndexError. Negative indexes can also be used inside slices.

code_examples.title: Negative Index
code_examples.code:
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40]
print(numbers[-1])
print(numbers[-2])
code_examples.explanation: -1 points to the last element and -2 to the second-last element.

questions.question: What is a list comprehension?

answer.short_answer: A list comprehension is a concise way to create a new list by applying an expression to items from an iterable, optionally filtering them with a condition.
answer.detailed_explanation: The common form is [expression for item in iterable if condition]. It replaces many simple loops with a compact expression. List comprehensions are useful for straightforward transformations and filtering. If the logic becomes complicated or requires multiple side effects, a normal for loop is usually easier to read. The result is always a new list.

code_examples.title: Basic
code_examples.code:
squares = [x * x for x in range(5)]
print(squares)
code_examples.explanation: Each number is transformed into its square.

code_examples.title: With Condition
code_examples.code:
even = [x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]
print(even)
code_examples.explanation: Only numbers satisfying the condition are included.

questions.question: What is dictionary comprehension?

answer.short_answer: Dictionary comprehension is a concise way to build a dictionary from an iterable using key:value expressions, optionally with a condition.
answer.detailed_explanation: The general form is {key_expression: value_expression for item in iterable if condition}. It is useful when keys and values can be generated from existing data in a simple transformation. It creates a new dictionary. As with list comprehensions, keep the expression readable rather than forcing complicated business logic into one line.

code_examples.title: Squares Dictionary
code_examples.code:
squares = {x: x * x for x in range(1, 4)}
print(squares)
code_examples.explanation: Each number becomes a key and its square becomes the value.

questions.question: What is set comprehension?

answer.short_answer: Set comprehension creates a set from an iterable using an expression and optional condition. Duplicate results are automatically stored only once.
answer.detailed_explanation: Set comprehension has a form similar to list comprehension but uses set braces and produces a set. Because sets contain unique elements, repeated results are removed. It is useful for generating unique transformed values or filtered values. The resulting set should not be treated as a positional sequence.

code_examples.title: Unique Results
code_examples.explanation: The duplicate input produces the same result, but a set keeps each result only once.

questions.question: What is the difference between copy() and deepcopy()?

answer.short_answer: A shallow copy creates a new outer object but shares nested objects; a deep copy recursively copies nested objects so they can be changed independently.
answer.detailed_explanation: copy.copy() and methods such as list.copy() create shallow copies. This is enough when nested objects do not need to be independent. copy.deepcopy() recursively copies nested mutable structures. With nested lists or dictionaries, this difference is important because modifying a shared nested object through a shallow copy can also change what you see through the original. Deep copying can use more memory and time.

code_examples.title: Shallow Copy
code_examples.code:
import copy
a = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
b = copy.copy(a)
b[0].append(99)
print(a)
code_examples.explanation: The nested list is shared between a and b.

code_examples.title: Deep Copy
code_examples.code:
import copy
a = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
b = copy.deepcopy(a)
b[0].append(99)
print(a)
print(b)
code_examples.explanation: Nested objects are copied independently.

questions.question: What is shallow copy in Python?

answer.short_answer: A shallow copy creates a new outer container but keeps references to the same nested objects.
answer.detailed_explanation: For a nested structure, a shallow copy separates only the top-level object. If the nested object is mutable, both the original and the shallow copy can still point to that same nested object. You can create shallow copies with copy.copy(), list.copy(), or list slicing for lists. Shallow copying is often enough for flat data, but nested mutable data needs more care.

code_examples.title: Nested Object Shared
code_examples.code:
a = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
b = a.copy()
b[0].append(5)
print(a)
print(b)
code_examples.explanation: The outer lists are different, but the nested first list is shared.

questions.question: What is deep copy in Python?

answer.short_answer: A deep copy recursively creates copies of nested objects so that mutable nested state is independent from the original.
answer.detailed_explanation: copy.deepcopy() is useful when you need a completely independent nested structure. It recursively copies objects that it can copy, while handling shared references and recursive structures according to the copy module rules. Deep copying can be more expensive than shallow copying, so it should be used when independent nested state is actually needed.

code_examples.title: Independent Nested Data
code_examples.code:
import copy
a = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
b = copy.deepcopy(a)
b[0].append(5)
print(a)
print(b)
code_examples.explanation: Changing the nested list in b does not affect a.

questions.question: What is the difference between None, 0, False, and an empty string?

answer.short_answer: None means absence of a value, 0 is an integer, False is a Boolean, and an empty string is a string with no characters. They are different values and types, although all are falsy in Boolean contexts.
answer.detailed_explanation: None has type NoneType and is commonly used to represent missing, unavailable, or intentionally absent data. 0 is an integer numeric value, False is a Boolean value, and "" is an empty string. They should not be treated as interchangeable just because bool() returns False for each. In particular, use value is None when you specifically mean to test for None.

code_examples.title: Different Types
code_examples.code:
print(type(None))
print(type(0))
print(type(False))
print(type(''))
code_examples.explanation: The four values have different types.

questions.question: What are truthy and falsy values in Python?

answer.short_answer: Truthy values behave like True in Boolean contexts, while falsy values behave like False. Common falsy values include None, False, zero, and empty strings or collections.
answer.detailed_explanation: Python evaluates an object’s truth value in if, while, and Boolean expressions. Common falsy values include None, False, 0, 0.0, 0j, "", [], (), {}, and set(). Most other objects are truthy unless their type defines different behavior. bool(value) can be used to see the truth value explicitly. This concept is frequently used for checking whether a collection has data.

code_examples.title: Falsy
code_examples.code:
print(bool(0))
print(bool(''))
print(bool([]))
code_examples.explanation: Zero, an empty string, and an empty list are falsy.

code_examples.title: Truthy
code_examples.code:
print(bool(10))
print(bool('Python'))
print(bool([1]))
code_examples.explanation: Non-zero numbers and non-empty objects are normally truthy.

questions.question: What are membership operators in Python?

answer.short_answer: The membership operators are in and not in. They check whether a value is contained in an iterable or collection.
answer.detailed_explanation: in returns True when the value is found, and not in returns True when it is not found. For lists and strings, membership generally searches through the sequence. For sets and dictionaries, membership is based on their collection semantics and is typically efficient. For dictionaries, value in dictionary checks keys by default, not values.

code_examples.title: List Membership
code_examples.code:
numbers = [10, 20, 30]
print(20 in numbers)
print(40 not in numbers)
code_examples.explanation: 20 exists in the list, while 40 does not.

code_examples.title: Dictionary Membership
code_examples.explanation: Dictionary membership checks keys by default.

questions.question: What are identity operators in Python?

answer.short_answer: The identity operators are is and is not. They check whether two references point to the same object.
answer.detailed_explanation: Identity is different from equality. == asks whether two objects are equal according to their equality operation, while is asks whether they are the exact same object. The safest common use of is is checking singleton objects such as None: if value is None. Do not use is as a general replacement for == when comparing values.

code_examples.title: Same Object
code_examples.code:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
print(a is b)
code_examples.explanation: Both names refer to the same list object.

code_examples.title: Equal but Different
code_examples.code:
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
print(a == b)
print(a is b)
code_examples.explanation: The contents are equal, but the list objects are different.

questions.question: What is operator precedence in Python?

answer.short_answer: Operator precedence determines the order in which operators are evaluated in an expression. Parentheses can be used to make the desired order explicit.
answer.detailed_explanation: For example, multiplication has higher precedence than addition, so 2 + 3 * 4 becomes 2 + (3 * 4). Python defines precedence rules for arithmetic, comparisons, Boolean operators, and other operators. In interviews, explain the idea and use parentheses when an expression could be unclear. Parentheses improve readability even when you know the precedence rules.

code_examples.title: Precedence
code_examples.code:
result = 2 + 3 * 4
print(result)
code_examples.explanation: Multiplication is evaluated before addition.

code_examples.title: Parentheses
code_examples.code:
result = (2 + 3) * 4
print(result)
code_examples.explanation: Parentheses force addition to happen first.

questions.question: What is the difference between /, //, %, and ** operators?

answer.short_answer: / performs true division, // performs floor division, % returns the remainder, and ** performs exponentiation.
answer.detailed_explanation: These operators have distinct numerical purposes. / normally produces a floating-point result. // performs floor division, meaning it rounds down toward negative infinity. % returns the remainder associated with division. ** raises the left operand to a power. A common interview trap is negative floor division: -7 // 2 is -4, not -3, because floor means toward negative infinity.

code_examples.title: Four Operators
code_examples.code:
print(7 / 2)
print(7 // 2)
print(7 % 2)
print(2 ** 3)
code_examples.explanation: The results show true division, floor division, remainder, and exponentiation.

code_examples.title: Negative Floor Division
code_examples.code: print(-7 // 2)
code_examples.explanation: Floor division moves toward negative infinity.

questions.question: What is the difference between and, or, and not?

answer.short_answer: and combines conditions requiring the left side and the needed right side to be truthy, or returns a truthy result when the first truthy operand is found, and not reverses a truth value.
answer.detailed_explanation: Python’s Boolean operators are short-circuiting and return operands rather than always returning Boolean values. and stops at the first falsy operand and otherwise returns the last operand. or stops at the first truthy operand and otherwise returns the last operand. not always returns a Boolean value. This behavior is important for conditions and default-value patterns.

code_examples.title: Conditions
code_examples.code:
age = 21
has_id = True
print(age >= 18 and has_id)
print(age < 18 or has_id)
print(not has_id)
code_examples.explanation: and combines requirements, or accepts either side, and not reverses the truth value.

questions.question: What is short-circuit evaluation in Python?

answer.short_answer: Short-circuit evaluation means Python stops evaluating a Boolean expression as soon as the final result is known. and stops on a falsy operand; or stops on a truthy operand.
answer.detailed_explanation: Short-circuiting is useful for efficiency and for safely controlling whether a later expression runs. For example, in x != 0 and 10 / x, the division is skipped when x is zero, preventing a division-by-zero exception. With or, a common pattern is value or default, where default is evaluated only if value is falsy. Remember that and and or return operands, not necessarily True or False.

code_examples.title: Safe and
code_examples.code:
x = 0
result = x != 0 and 10 / x
print(result)
code_examples.explanation: The second expression is never evaluated because the first condition is false.

code_examples.title: Default with or
code_examples.code:
name = ''
print(name or 'Guest')
code_examples.explanation: Because name is falsy, the right side is returned.

questions.question: What is the difference between range() and a list?

answer.short_answer: range() represents an immutable sequence of integers without materializing all values as a list, while a list stores its elements and can be modified.
answer.detailed_explanation: range(start, stop, step) is especially useful for loops and large numeric sequences because it is memory-efficient. It represents the sequence rather than creating a full list of all integers. A list actually stores its elements and supports mutation. Convert range to a list with list(range(...)) when you need a real list object.

code_examples.title: range()
code_examples.code:
for i in range(3):
    print(i)
code_examples.explanation: range(3) represents 0, 1, and 2.

code_examples.title: Convert to List
code_examples.code:
numbers = list(range(3))
print(numbers)
code_examples.explanation: list() materializes the values into a mutable list.

questions.question: What is unpacking in Python?

answer.short_answer: Unpacking assigns elements from an iterable to multiple variables in one statement. Extended unpacking with * can collect multiple remaining elements.
answer.detailed_explanation: Basic unpacking requires a compatible number of values and target variables. Extended unpacking allows one target to collect the remaining values into a list. Unpacking is commonly used with tuples, lists, function return values, and loops. It makes code concise while keeping the structure of the data visible.

code_examples.title: Basic Unpacking
code_examples.code:
person = ('Abhi', 21)
name, age = person
print(name)
print(age)
code_examples.explanation: The two tuple values are assigned to the two variables.

code_examples.title: Extended Unpacking
code_examples.code:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]
first, *middle, last = numbers
print(first)
print(middle)
print(last)
code_examples.explanation: The starred target collects the remaining elements into a list.

questions.question: What is the difference between split(), join(), and replace()?

answer.short_answer: split() breaks a string into parts, join() combines an iterable of strings, and replace() substitutes one substring with another.
answer.detailed_explanation: split() is commonly used to turn text into a list of pieces using a delimiter. join() performs the opposite kind of operation by combining strings with a separator. replace() creates a new string with matching text replaced. Because strings are immutable, none of these methods changes the original string object in place.

code_examples.title: split()
code_examples.code:
text = 'Python is easy'
print(text.split())
code_examples.explanation: Whitespace is used as the default separator.

code_examples.title: join()
code_examples.code:
words = ['Python', 'is', 'easy']
print(' '.join(words))
code_examples.explanation: The space is used to join the strings.

code_examples.title: replace()
code_examples.code:
text = 'I like Java'
text = text.replace('Java', 'Python')
print(text)
code_examples.explanation: replace() returns a new string containing the replacement.

questions.question: What is the difference between find() and index() in strings?

answer.short_answer: Both search for a substring and return its starting index. find() returns -1 if it is absent, while index() raises ValueError.
answer.detailed_explanation: Use find() when absence is a normal possibility and you want a numeric sentinel result. Use index() when not finding the substring should be treated as an error. Both return the first matching position and support optional start and end boundaries. This difference is a common interview follow-up because the normal successful behavior is the same.

code_examples.title: find()
code_examples.code:
text = 'Python'
print(text.find('th'))
print(text.find('xyz'))
code_examples.explanation: find() returns the position or -1 when there is no match.

code_examples.title: index()
code_examples.code:
text = 'Python'
print(text.index('th'))
# text.index('xyz')  # ValueError
code_examples.explanation: index() returns the position when found and raises ValueError when it is not found.

questions.question: What is the difference between %, str.format(), and f-strings?

answer.short_answer: %, str.format(), and f-strings are different string-formatting styles. f-strings are the modern concise style for embedding expressions, while format() and % formatting are also found in existing Python code.
answer.detailed_explanation: Percent formatting is an older style using placeholders such as %s. str.format() uses braces and a format() call. F-strings prefix the string with f and allow expressions directly inside braces. F-strings are generally the most readable modern choice when supported by the project’s Python version. Knowing all three is useful because interviews and real codebases may contain each style.

code_examples.title: Percent Formatting
code_examples.code:
name = 'Abhi'
print('Hello %s' % name)
code_examples.explanation: The %s placeholder is replaced by the supplied value.

code_examples.title: str.format()
code_examples.code:
name = 'Abhi'
age = 21
print('My name is {} and I am {} years old'.format(name, age))
code_examples.output: My name is Abhi and I am 21 years old
code_examples.explanation: format() replaces the braces with the supplied arguments.

code_examples.title: f-string
code_examples.code:
name = 'Abhi'
age = 21
print(f'My name is {name} and I am {age} years old')
code_examples.output: My name is Abhi and I am 21 years old
code_examples.explanation: f-strings embed variables or expressions directly inside braces.
